text:
**Position: Yes — posthumous harm is coherent, provided we give up an experiential theory of harm in favor of an interest-based one.**

**The puzzle**

The Epicurean challenge is real: harm seems to require a subject who bears it. Once someone is dead, there is no subject present to undergo any bad effect. So when a promise made to Jones is broken after Jones dies, there seems to be no one there to be wronged — not "dead Jones," since there's no such entity in any robust sense, and not "living Jones," since he no longer exists to receive anything, good or bad.

**Why the challenge fails**

The Epicurean argument only works if all harm must be *experienced*. But we already reject that view in ordinary cases. If your friend deceives you and you never find out — she mocks you behind your back, betrays a confidence, secretly disrespects the thing you asked her to protect — most people judge that you have been wronged and harmed, even though nothing in your conscious experience changes. What's been damaged is not your feelings but your *interest*: the state of affairs you cared about and had a stake in has been thwarted.

Once we accept that interests can be set back without any corresponding experience, the question of *timing* — whether the setback occurs before or after death — loses its special force. What made the secret-betrayal case count as harm wasn't that the victim was alive at the moment of betrayal in some experientially relevant sense; it's that the victim had, at some point, a genuine interest in the state of affairs in question. Death removes the *experiencer* but doesn't retroactively erase the fact that the interest existed and was constitutive of that person's life and agency.

**The metaphysical worry, defused**

The remaining objection is that this still requires a strange kind of backward action — harming someone who, at the time of harm, doesn't exist. But this misdescribes what's going on. Nothing is being done *to* a currently-existing dead person; nothing needs to travel backward in time. What happens is that a fact about the deceased's life — "Y's trust in X, formed and held while Y was alive, was honored/betrayed" — becomes true or false depending on events after Y's death. This is no odder than other cases where later events fix the truth of earlier-indexed claims (e.g., "Smith's prediction was vindicated" can only be evaluated once we know what happened later, without requiring Smith to exist now). The *bearer* of the interest is the antemortem person — the person as they existed across their life — not some ghostly postmortem entity. The harm is real, but it is of a different, non-experiential kind: a thwarting of interest rather than an infliction of suffering.

**What this implies for wills**

If this is right, the obligation to execute a person's will faithfully is not merely:
- a legal duty owed to the state,
- a duty owed to the living beneficiaries, or
- a matter of social convention that makes promise-keeping generally useful.

It is also a genuine moral duty owed *to the deceased themselves*. The testator had an interest — while alive — in how their property and wishes would be disposed of after death. Frustrating that will doesn't just disappoint the living or violate a legal formality; it wrongs the person who died, by defeating an interest that was central to how they tried to extend their agency past the limits of their own existence. This gives executors and heirs a stronger, more personal reason for fidelity than mere legal compliance — closer to the reason you have to keep a promise to a dying friend than to the reason you have to follow a statute.

**What this implies for posthumous reputation**

Likewise, defamation or distortion of the dead is not merely bad because it upsets grieving relatives or corrupts the historical record for its own sake. Many people have, while alive, a real and central interest in how their life's work and character will be understood afterward — that's why people write memoirs, seal letters, request certain facts stay private, or specify how they want to be remembered. If those interests are real components of a life, then betraying them posthumously (misrepresenting someone's work, publishing what they explicitly wanted destroyed, defaming their character after death) is a genuine harm to *them*, not just an offense against the living or against truth in the abstract.

**A caveat this view forces on us**

The harm, however, is not indefinitely weighty, nor equal to all harms in life. Because the "subject" is the interest-bearing life rather than an ongoing experiencer, the strength of the harm plausibly tracks two things: (1) how central the thwarted interest was to that person's self-conception and life-projects, and (2) how much of that interest-bearing life remains socially "live" — connected to people who knew them, records that persist, structures the person built. This is why betraying Julius Caesar's wishes today feels almost like a category error, while betraying your grandmother's explicit last wishes next year feels like a real wrong: the interest hasn't yet faded from the web of relationships and facts that gave it force. So the position implies a kind of *decaying* moral claim — real, but attenuating over time — rather than a permanent, undiminished right belonging to the dead.
